section_summary: This section documents U.S. concern over Japanese acquisition of strategic materials throughout the Americas, including copper, scrap iron, petroleum, aluminum, tungsten, vanadium, cotton, lignum vitae, and other ores. It combines intelligence reports and diplomatic correspondence with numerous congressional and public inquiries about continued exports to Japan, alongside State Department explanations of the export-licensing system. The section also covers Japanese commercial agent Koichiro Kuzutani’s activities in Haiti, El Salvador, and Nicaragua, German–East Asian trade through Manchuria, and a detailed proposal for restricting gasoline exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Military Intelligence summary on copper from the S.S. Biancamano
subfiles.about: Transmits a Military Intelligence Division summary concerning disposition of copper formerly carried by the S.S. Biancamano.
subfiles.summary: The brief confidential covering note forwards a March 5 intelligence summary to Assistant Secretary Berle. The enclosure concerns copper being rerouted through New York for ultimate shipment to Japan.

subfiles.title: Shipment of copper from the S.S. Biancamano
subfiles.doc_type: Military Intelligence Division summary of information
subfiles.to: Department of State and other agencies
subfiles.about: Reports arrangements to carry copper via three steamships from Cristóbal to New York in transit to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Three lots of roughly 300 tons each were assigned to the S.S. Cristobal, S.S. Ancon, and S.S. Panama, with Florencio E. Delgado acting locally and H. S. Dorf handling the New York arrangements. Bills of lading would describe the cargo as in transit for Yamahatsu Boeki Kaisha in Osaka. The report notes that the circuitous routing through New York was not understood.

subfiles.title: Feis memorandum on proposed purchase of Argentine scrap iron
subfiles.about: Recommends encouraging private American purchases of Argentine scrap without promising shipping in return.
subfiles.summary: Feis advises against a government commitment either to buy the scrap or to provide ships. He proposes giving Argentina a list of interested American firms, following the precedent used with the Dominican Republic, while stating only that shipping might be made available if circumstances permitted.

subfiles.title: Welles instruction to Bonsal on Argentine scrap iron
subfiles.about: Directs Bonsal to consult Feis and promote sale of Argentine scrap to American interests.
subfiles.summary: Welles calls attention to the final paragraph of Feis’s memorandum. He considers it highly desirable to facilitate an American purchase of the available scrap iron.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s note on Argentine proposal
subfiles.about: Requests prompt views on an Argentine proposal to exchange scrap iron for ships.
subfiles.summary: Welles states that the Argentine ambassador left the attached proposal with him. He suggests arranging for purchase of the scrap while limiting any shipping assurance to vessels that might later become available.

subfiles.title: Argentine Embassy note on exchanging scrap iron for ships
subfiles.about: Explains that Japan has offered ships in exchange for Argentina’s deteriorating stock of scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Argentina reports that its large stock of old iron is being lost through oxidation and that private Japanese agents have proposed a barter for ships. Because Argentina urgently needs shipping, it asks whether the United States could meet any part of that need and thereby obviate a Japanese transaction. The note also mentions Brazilian purchases of cargo ships and tankers in the United States.

subfiles.title: Firms actively purchasing scrap iron abroad
subfiles.about: Lists seven American firms or contacts reportedly active in foreign scrap-iron purchasing.
subfiles.summary: The list supplies names and addresses in Washington, Houston, New York City, and Jersey City. It was intended for possible use in connecting Argentine sellers with private American buyers.

subfiles.title: Argentine note regarding exchange of scrap iron for ships
subfiles.about: Assesses the Japanese barter proposal, American demand for scrap, and the lack of shipping available to Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum doubts Japan has ships to barter but confirms strong American commercial demand for scrap throughout Latin America. It concludes that the United States Government is not buying scrap and cannot make important tonnage available to Argentina. A case involving Alberto Dodero and the former San Bernardino illustrates how an Argentine-controlled ship ultimately passed through a New York broker to Japanese registry.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary intelligence summary on mineral shipments and Yugoslavia
subfiles.about: Contains fragmentary references to a mineral-supply mission connected with Japan and to Yugoslav views on defending Salonika.
subfiles.summary: The first surviving lines mention an arrival at Casablanca, ostensibly to arrange a mineral supply to Japan. A separate Yugoslavia item reports a favorable impression of the government and discussion of Yugoslav–Turkish cooperation against a German attack on Salonika.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Señor Pardo concerning Argentine scrap iron
subfiles.about: Records the Department’s response to Argentina’s proposed exchange of scrap iron for Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: Bonsal told Pardo that the United States had no ships available, was not buying scrap, and doubted Japan possessed suitable ships to exchange. He noted private American demand and offered a list of firms, which Pardo said he already had. Bonsal believed no further action was needed.

subfiles.title: Duggan memorandum on the Argentine ambassador’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Reports that the Argentine ambassador asked what consideration had been given to his scrap-iron proposal.
subfiles.summary: Duggan summarizes Bonsal’s discussion with Señor Pardo. Unless Welles wished to add further comment, Duggan proposed telling the ambassador that the Department had nothing more to add.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum of conversation with Señor Pardo
subfiles.about: Duplicates the account of Bonsal’s discussion with Pardo about scrap iron and shipping.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats that no American ships were available and that the Government was neither buying nor contemplating buying scrap iron. It also records doubts about Japanese shipping capacity and concludes that no further action was required.

subfiles.title: Editorial comments on an export-control form letter
subfiles.about: Suggests changes to standard language used in replies about export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The writer recommends reducing repeated use of the word “any.” He also prefers “in accordance with national defense needs” to language implying that the State Department merely follows the wishes of defense agencies.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram from Argentina on a shipment to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a separately filed telegram concerning a shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies the original as telegram 321, sent from Argentina by Armour. It directs researchers to defense file 811.20 Defense (4)/1720.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Far Eastern Affairs communication
subfiles.about: Refers to an original communication filed under 894.00/1031.
subfiles.summary: The subject is illegible in the surviving OCR. The sheet records Davies of Far Eastern Affairs as the originating official and supplies the alternate file number.

subfiles.title: Beckworth inquiry concerning exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests comment on a constituent’s criticism of American oil and scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Beckworth quotes a constituent who contrasts American sympathy and financial support for China with the continued provision of strategic supplies to Japan. He asks the Secretary for comments on the allegation.

subfiles.title: Reply to Representative Beckworth on oil and scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory export-control system governing petroleum products and scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that aviation gasoline, lubricating oil, scrap iron, and many other products require special licenses under the act of July 2, 1940. Licenses are refused when a shipment would harm national defense. He adds that both the controlled-products list and licensing policy are continually revised.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting prohibition of an aluminum export at Manzanillo
subfiles.about: Reports that customs authorities received orders from Mexico City not to permit a specified aluminum shipment to be exported.
subfiles.summary: The Manzanillo customs chief was instructed by Mexico City to stop the aluminum export mentioned in an earlier telegram. The message is marked for close paraphrase before disclosure.

subfiles.title: Despatch concerning Koichiro Kuzutani’s visa application
subfiles.about: Transmits a letter from Kuzutani explaining that he obtained a U.S. visa in the Dominican Republic.
subfiles.summary: The despatch follows an earlier report about Kuzutani’s application for a temporary visitor’s visa. White notes that Kuzutani is now in New York after obtaining the visa in the Dominican Republic and encloses his letter.

subfiles.title: Kuzutani letter withdrawing his visa request
subfiles.about: States that Kuzutani secured a visa at Ciudad Trujillo and no longer needs action from the Port-au-Prince consulate.
subfiles.summary: Kuzutani recounts applying at Port-au-Prince on March 24 and then traveling to Ciudad Trujillo because urgent business prevented him from waiting. After receiving a visa there and returning to the United States, he asks that the Haitian application be discontinued.

subfiles.title: Engel referral of Haase inquiry on iron ore shipments
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s request for information about possible American iron-ore shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative Engel transmits a letter from E. Hughey Haase of Muskegon. He requests information with which to answer Haase’s questions promptly.

subfiles.title: Haase letter questioning iron-ore exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether the United States continues sending iron ore to Japan and why it would do so while favoring China.
subfiles.summary: Haase cites public discussion of iron-ore shipments and asks whether fear of Japan or the influence of industry explains them. He says the question is shared by numerous people in Muskegon.

subfiles.title: Reply to Engel concerning iron-ore exports
subfiles.about: Explains that iron ore, scrap, and other iron and steel products require export licenses, including for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department assures Engel that no license is issued for a shipment believed detrimental to national defense. It emphasizes that controlled-product lists and licensing policy are constantly adjusted and returns Haase’s letter.

subfiles.title: Sparkman referral of Maxwell inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards Reverend W. P. Maxwell’s questions about Japanese purchases of oil and copper.
subfiles.summary: Sparkman asks the Department for information enabling him to answer Maxwell. Maxwell’s original letter is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Maxwell letter on Japanese purchases of oil and copper
subfiles.about: Questions reports that Japanese naval tankers obtain American oil and that Japan buys scarce copper on the spot market.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell argues that such trade appears inconsistent with presidential promises of aid to the democracies and China. He asks why the situation is permitted and how official policy can be reconciled with actual conduct.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Hill concerning Maxwell’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Explains licensing rules for petroleum and copper exports and their application to Japanese naval tankers.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that specified petroleum products and copper require special export licenses and that shipments harmful to defense interests are denied. The use of naval tankers does not remove the licensing requirement, except for legitimate ships’ stores consumed during the voyage. Maxwell’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Reply to Representative Sparkman concerning Maxwell’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Provides the State Department’s explanation of controls on oil and copper exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that copper and certain petroleum products require special licenses and that defense-damaging exports are not authorized. It also clarifies that Japanese naval tankers remain subject to export controls, apart from ordinary ships’ stores.

subfiles.title: Congressional referral of Charles V. Hendel’s oil inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards a New Haven constituent’s question about sending oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page is largely obscured, but it belongs to the referral answered by the Department on May 8. The attached inquiry was from Charles V. Hendel.

subfiles.title: Hendel postcard questioning oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks why oil is being sent to Japan despite its membership in the Axis.
subfiles.summary: Hendel warns that exported oil could later be used against the United States. The brief message requests an explanation of the policy.

subfiles.title: Reply to Shanley concerning oil sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains controls on aviation gasoline, lubricating oil, and other exports in response to Hendel’s inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that controlled petroleum exports require individual licenses and that proposals detrimental to national defense are refused. He notes that export schedules and licensing policies remain subject to revision and returns Hendel’s letter.

subfiles.title: British Embassy transmittal on Mexican mineral shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards details comparing advance information with the minerals actually loaded for Japan in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Marris recalls information previously passed to Dean Acheson about lead and other mineral shipments. He encloses a memorandum showing the cargo ultimately loaded.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of minerals loaded in Mexico for Japan
subfiles.about: Lists lead, zinc, vanadium concentrates, mercury, and antimony loaded for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies shippers and gives quantities, including more than 4,000 tons of lead, 1,150 tons of zinc, vanadium concentrates, mercury, and antimony. It explains that roughly 100 additional tons of vanadium had to be resacked because the original containers deteriorated in storage.

subfiles.title: Finletter acknowledgment to Marris
subfiles.about: Thanks Marris for the memorandum on mineral shipments from Mexico to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Finletter acknowledges receipt of Marris’s April 15 memorandum. The short reply contains no additional substantive discussion.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary British Embassy routing page
subfiles.about: Records receipt and routing of a largely illegible communication addressed to Finletter.
subfiles.summary: Only departmental stamps, a file number, and Finletter’s name remain legible. The substantive text cannot be recovered from the OCR.

subfiles.title: Senator Hill referral of Maxwell’s strategic-materials letter
subfiles.about: Forwards Reverend Maxwell’s letter concerning strategic-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hill calls the enclosure self-explanatory and asks for a report. This referral prompted the Department’s May 12 response.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Maxwell letter on oil and copper exports
subfiles.about: Repeats Maxwell’s questions about Japanese acquisition of American petroleum and copper.
subfiles.summary: Although heavily degraded, the page is another copy of Maxwell’s Sheffield letter. It challenges the consistency of supporting China while strategic supplies remain available to Japan.

subfiles.title: McLaughlin referral of Potter gasoline inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards A. C. Potter’s questions about gasoline exports to Japan and their consistency with support for China.
subfiles.summary: McLaughlin asks for information with which to answer his constituent. He requests return of the enclosed letter after it has served its purpose.

subfiles.title: Potter letter concerning gasoline exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Questions reports that nearly 600,000 barrels of gasoline were shipped to Japan in 1940.
subfiles.summary: Potter regards continued licensing of gasoline exports as potentially contradictory to American support for China. He asks for the reason behind the policy and what citizens can do if the procedure is unsound.

subfiles.title: McLaughlin acknowledgment of Hull’s reply
subfiles.about: Thanks Hull for the Department’s response concerning Potter’s gasoline inquiry.
subfiles.summary: McLaughlin acknowledges Hull’s May 9 letter. He states that he will send a copy to Potter for his information.

subfiles.title: Reply to McLaughlin concerning gasoline shipments
subfiles.about: Explains the export-licensing regime for aviation gasoline, lubricating oil, and other petroleum products.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that controlled petroleum products require special licenses and that licenses are denied where shipments would harm national defense. He adds that export controls and licensing policy are continually adjusted as conditions change.

subfiles.title: Federal Bureau of Investigation routing sheet
subfiles.about: Records departmental receipt and routing of an FBI communication with enclosures.
subfiles.summary: The substantive subject is illegible in the OCR. Stamps show routing through the State Department’s commercial-affairs offices and filing under 894.24/1363.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese offer for Bolivian tungsten
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram reporting a Japanese offer for Bolivia’s entire tungsten production.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to telegram 67 from Bolivia. The original was filed under 811.20 Defense (M)/1837.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Bolivian tungsten negotiations
subfiles.about: Refers to information from Bolivian ministers concerning tungsten negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies telegram 69 from Bolivia. It directs readers to defense file 811.20 Defense (M)/1867.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Netherlands East Indies bauxite exports
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram reporting bauxite exports from the Netherlands East Indies and the 1941 quota.
subfiles.summary: The note cites exports of approximately 104,000 tons during 1940 compared with 115,000 tons in 1939. It also mentions a monthly 1941 quota of 30,000 tons and points to file 894.6359/1.

subfiles.title: Emily G. Balch letter on exports useful to Japan
subfiles.about: Expresses distress over continued supplies of materials useful to Japan and asks why they cannot be stopped.
subfiles.summary: Although portions are difficult to read, Balch is plainly concerned that exports continue despite Japan’s use of such supplies. She asks Hornbeck for an explanation of the government’s policy.

subfiles.title: Reply to Emily G. Balch on export controls
subfiles.about: Explains the Export Control Act and the broader policy considerations governing trade restrictions against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department describes the President’s authority to prohibit or curtail selected exports in the interest of national defense and encloses information on applicable regulations. It adds that policy toward trade with Japan requires balancing complicated international, legal, and domestic considerations.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of Miletznik letter
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent’s request for information about exports to Japan and asks for a report.
subfiles.summary: The Senate form forwards the attached communication for favorable consideration. It requests return of the enclosure together with the Department’s report.

subfiles.title: Miletznik request for a list of exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests a list of petroleum, metals, and other materials exported to Japan by the United States and other American republics.
subfiles.summary: Miletznik advocates an embargo, arguing that exported materials sustain Japan’s war in China and could later be used against American forces. He characterizes the combination of strategic exports and costly naval expansion as hypocritical.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Mead concerning trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes licensing controls on iron, steel, nonferrous metals, and petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that many strategic products may be exported only under special license and that harmful shipments are denied. Copies of Export Control Schedules One through Four are enclosed, and Miletznik’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Japanese purchases of lignum vitae in Nicaragua
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese efforts to buy lignum vitae and alleged Guardia profiteering in the Sébaco district.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source claims that Japanese buyers are acquiring all obtainable lignum vitae, much of it from Sébaco. The local Guardia captain allegedly coerces or steals supplies and resells them in Managua at a large profit. President Somoza is said to tolerate such graft as a means of retaining senior Guardia loyalty.

subfiles.title: Shipments from and to Germany through Manzhouli during March 1941
subfiles.from: A. S. Chase, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Lists German machinery and military equipment entering Manchuria and commodities shipped west to Germany via the Trans-Siberian Railway.
subfiles.summary: Inbound cargo reportedly included locomotives, tractors, trucks, submarines, tube-rolling equipment, tools, magnetos, and machinery for aircraft-part production. Outbound shipments included soybeans, soybean oil, fats, whale oil, rags, and rubber. Chase asks whether the British-derived intelligence can be supplied through Tokyo, Washington, or London to avoid duplication and exposure of the Dairen source.

subfiles.title: Report on Koichiro Kuzutani’s activities in El Salvador
subfiles.about: Describes Kuzutani’s Salvadoran visit and proposed barter of Japanese goods for raw cotton.
subfiles.summary: Kuzutani arrived from Brownsville on February 28, stayed in San Salvador until March 7, and then flew to Managua. The Legation believes his trip concerned an unsuccessful compensation deal exchanging Japanese manufactures for Salvadoran cotton. No political or subversive activity was discovered.

subfiles.title: Control of gasoline exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s gasoline supply and proposes sharply restricting American exports capable of conversion to aviation fuel.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum compares Japanese gasoline imports from the United States and Netherlands East Indies, explains the Batavia contracts, and notes that U.S. licenses issued during the previous eight months covered more than 9.2 million barrels. It warns that Japan depends heavily on American gasoline that can be raised to aviation grade and that accumulating stocks may indicate preparation for a major military operation. Proposed options are limiting exports to 500,000 barrels annually or lowering the permitted octane ceiling to 70, preferably as part of wider Anglo-American-Dutch cooperation.

subfiles.title: Activities of Koichiro Kuzutani in Nicaragua
subfiles.about: Reports Kuzutani’s Nicaraguan contacts and Japanese purchases of cotton, cottonseed, and lignum vitae.
subfiles.summary: Kuzutani stayed in Nicaragua from March 7 to March 21 and worked chiefly with Mitsui agent Domingo Calero before proceeding to Panama. Purchases attributed jointly to Kuzutani and Daisaku Hayashi included 1.7 million pounds of cotton, 900 tons of cottonseed, and nearly 300 tons of lignum vitae, mostly through compensation deals. No abnormal activity was proved, although Calero reportedly suspected from Kuzutani’s bearing that he was a military officer.

subfiles.title: FBI report on aluminum tanks exported from Mexico to Japan
subfiles.about: Traces four large aluminum tanks from a Mexican steel company through an alleged dummy buyer to export at Manzanillo for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The tanks, weighing 14,600 kilograms, were purchased nominally by Jaime Chermitzky but reportedly for A. Z. Phillips, then consigned through Antonio Llorena for Yokohama. Their costly shipment intact rather than as scrap is treated as suspicious. The report also identifies Mexican political and military figures with financial interests in the American Export Company and suggests possible Japanese backing.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Ambassador in Mexico quoting aluminum report
subfiles.about: Provides the embassy with the FBI report on aluminum tanks shipped through Manzanillo for Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: The instruction reproduces the allegations concerning Chermitzky, Phillips, the intact aluminum tanks, and the American Export Company. It emphasizes the suspected use of a dummy purchaser and the possibility of Japanese financial participation in a company linked to prominent Mexican figures.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Lima on Japanese purchases of Peruvian ores and cotton
subfiles.about: Warns of persistent Japanese bids for Peruvian minerals and extensive contracting for the 1941 cotton crop.
subfiles.summary: Major firms report refusing Japanese offers of high prices for all types and quantities of ores and concentrates, but smaller producers may accept them unless control is established quickly. Japanese purchasers are estimated to have contracted about 80,000 bales, or 20 percent of Peru’s 1941 cotton crop. Norweb warns that their use of dollar exchange is giving Japan substantial economic influence among Peruvian producers.
